title: Type I for Parents and Educators: Nine Ideas for Helping Our Kids
coreMove: Parents and educators protect motivation by pairing expectations with choice, useful feedback, effort praise, and meaningful work.

exampleSpecs.audience: Orla, a teacher redesigning homework without lowering standards
exampleSpecs.stakes: A homework review has to separate meaningful practice from busywork.

exampleSpecs.audience: Bennett, a parent separating allowance from contribution
exampleSpecs.stakes: A family conversation could turn every chore into a transaction.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show family contribution without a simple pay-for-everything bargain.

exampleSpecs.audience: Zara, a student choosing a science fair project
exampleSpecs.stakes: A science fair can become trophy chasing or real inquiry.

exampleSpecs.audience: Micah, a teacher changing praise in a conference
exampleSpecs.stakes: A parent-teacher meeting could praise fixed smartness and make challenge risky.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Apply Dweck's praise research to feedback.

exampleSpecs.audience: Liora, a program lead keeping a showcase from becoming prize chasing
exampleSpecs.stakes: An after-school project event needs accountability without hollow competition.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show a delivery moment that protects curiosity.

exampleSpecs.audience: Hale, a teacher writing feedback that points to the next strategy
exampleSpecs.stakes: A feedback conference can judge a child or teach the next move.
